paragraphs.text: III. On Saint Athanasius.
Book I.

You are forcing us, Constantius, to condemn our fellow priest, the devout Athanasius, in his absence; but divine law forbids us to do this. With your royal authority you drive the priests of the Lord far and wide to shed blood, not knowing that you have tried to take from our minds the rules of justice that God handed down to us. Or will you be able to claim that God permits a man to be condemned when he is absent, unheard, and—what matters most—innocent? For how do you suppose God permits the unheard to be punished, when you see that Adam and Eve, the first parents of our race, were heard before they were struck by God's sentence? "And God called Adam and said to him, 'Adam, where are you?' And he said, 'I heard your voice, Lord, in paradise, and I was afraid because I am naked, and I hid myself.' And God said to him, 'Who told you that you were naked, unless you have eaten from the tree from which I had commanded you not to eat, that one alone?' And Adam said, 'The woman whom you gave me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate.' And God said to the woman, 'Why have you done this?' And the woman said, 'The serpent persuaded me, and I ate.'" Since, then, you see that God gave this pattern of judging, and since you gather from the sacred fountains of Scripture that God pronounced sentence only after they had been called out of hiding and had confessed, how impudent were you, and are you still, to give the servants of God a pattern of judging that did not come from the law of the Lord? Were you not afraid that we might say to God about you what was said about that renegade angel, "The serpent persuaded me"—namely, "The emperor Constantius led us astray; we believed him because we took him for a man"? Could you not see that you might be struck by the same sentence of God's indignation by which the serpent too was clearly struck? To him it is said: "Because you have done this, cursed are you above all cattle and all the beasts of the earth that are upon the earth; on your breast and belly you shall crawl, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life. And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed; he will watch for your head, and you will watch for his heel." Ought you not to have remembered from this one sentence of the Lord that you too could incur God's displeasure just as that angel incurred it, especially since you knew that your own work also was the serpent's work? Or, since that serpent was made from among the angels, did you suppose that you could become a serpent from among men? Not at all. But I wish you would tell me what difference there is between your deed and the deed of that renegade, apostate angel. If he deceived simple people by a lie, so do you—and indeed you deceive people who are not simple. If he enticed their minds to eat the fruit of the tree for the sake of their advantage, so do you, since you claim that you do it for the sake of peace.

And since you have said that you undertook this work for the good of all Christians, surely, once your works are examined, it becomes plain that you have imitated that serpent. Wanting us to become transgressors of God's commandments, you gave orders that a man be condemned absent and unheard, and that a hearing be refused to one who cried out that he could clear himself of the charge brought against him. The righteous Abel is killed, and Cain is questioned before he receives his sentence; and do you want a priest of the Lord to be punished unheard? "Abel," it says, "became a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground. And it came to pass after some days that Cain offered a sacrifice to the Lord from the fruit of the ground, and Abel too offered from the firstlings of his sheep; and God looked upon Abel and his gifts, but upon Cain and his sacrifices he did not look. And Cain was very sad, and his face fell. And the Lord God said to Cain, 'Why have you become sad, and why has your face fallen? Why did you not offer rightly? You have sinned; be still,'" and so on; and further on: "Cain said to Abel his brother, 'Let us go into the field.' And it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother and killed him. And God said to Cain, 'Where is your brother?' And he said, 'I do not know; am I my brother's keeper?' And God said, 'What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me from the ground.'" Was God not free to punish Cain before summoning and questioning him? But he did not wish to, giving us a pattern for how we should go about judging those entrusted to us—to us, I say, of whom he speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the peoples dedicated to his majesty: "And I will give you shepherds after my own heart, and they will feed you, feeding you with discipline." "Condemn," you say, "a man whom you do not know to have done wrong." Why? Clearly so that we should deserve to be called no longer bishops but madmen and executioners. Do you not fear, I ask, when you command such things, the voice of the Lord saying to the most holy Noah: "As the green plants, I have given you all things. Only flesh with the blood of its life you shall not eat. For I will require your blood, the blood of your lives, from the hands of every beast; I will require the life of man. Whoever sheds the blood of man, for the blood of man his blood shall be shed, for I made man in the image of God"? Do you not fear, I ask—you who see that you have become the killer of so many servants of God—that you are still slaughtering the innocent yourself and forcing us to become partners in your killings? When Moses was asked by his father-in-law Jethro why he kept the people waiting all day, he said, "The people come to me seeking judgment from God." If, then, the judgment of God's bishops ought to be so just that it can be said to have been settled by God's own judgment, how could you order us to condemn a man unheard, when you have found that Moses said, "The people come to me seeking judgment from the Lord"? If the people flock to us precisely in order to be judged according to God's law, why do you say, "Condemn an innocent man"? Therefore, since this command that you have issued does not come from the law of God but is plainly grounded in the will of the devil, understand at last who you are.

Lot's wife was turned into salt because she failed to carry out what she had been commanded. Would no harm befall us—thanks, I suppose, to your intervention, since you are, of course, the ruler of the Roman Empire—if we condemned a man weighed down by false charges? Sacred Scripture says in Exodus: "Moses went up to the mountain of God, and God called him from the mountain, saying: 'Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob and declare to the children of Israel: You yourselves have seen how much I did to the Egyptians, and I lifted you up as on eagles' wings and brought you to myself. And now, if you will truly hear my voice and keep my covenant, you will be to me a people abounding above all nations. For all the earth is mine. And you will be to me a most holy kingdom and a holy nation.'" How a holy nation, if we become murderers of the innocent? How a kingdom most holy to God, if we pass over his commandments? Again God says: "You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not bear false witness against your neighbor." You say the opposite: "Believe me when I tell you lies, and slaughter an innocent man." God warns in Exodus: "You shall not believe an idle report; you shall not agree with the wicked to become an unjust witness; you shall not join the many in wickedness. You shall not side with the many, turning aside with the crowd so as to pervert judgment, and you shall not show pity to the poor man in his case"; and further on: "You shall not pervert the judgment of the poor man in his case; you shall keep away from every unjust word; you shall not kill the innocent and the righteous; you shall not acquit the ungodly for bribes; for bribes blind the eyes of those who see and corrupt just words." Against these precepts, in order to set them aside, you compel God's servants to pervert his judgment, trying even with bribes to corrupt our upright conscience, which is dedicated to God. "If you will truly hear my voice," says God, "and do all that I tell you, I will be an enemy to your enemies and will oppose your adversaries." Now it is up to you to prove that God commanded the innocent to be struck down, the apostolic faith to be abandoned, and your faithlessness to be embraced. Why did you think that things contrary to the Lord's commandments should be ordered done? Especially since you remember that in Leviticus the Lord said to Moses: "Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: I am the Lord your God. You shall not act according to the practices of the land of Egypt, where you lived, and you shall not act there according to the practices of the land of the Canaanites, into which I will bring you, nor shall you walk in their ordinances. You shall carry out my judgments and keep my precepts and walk in them. I am the Lord your God. Keep all my precepts and all my judgments and do them; the man who does them shall live by them. I am the Lord your God." If you can show that it is written in the Lord's precepts that the righteous are to be punished at the prompting of the unrighteous, you may conclude that you have acted and are acting rightly in everything. Show that it is written in God's commandments that his worshipers, when assailed with slanders, are to be put to death by you, the persecutor of his house, through us bishops.

Why were you led by your fellow Arians into carrying out this malice? What reason compelled you, an emperor, to attack a man of God with slanders? Had you not read in Leviticus that God said: "Do not assail anyone with lies, and do not slander each his neighbor"? And further on: "You shall not lie, nor slander your neighbor, and you shall not profane the name of the Lord your God. I am the Lord your God. You shall not harm your neighbor, and you shall fear the Lord your God. I am the Lord your God. You shall do no injustice in judgment; you shall not show partiality to the person of the poor, nor be overawed by the person of the mighty; in righteousness you shall judge your neighbor. You shall not walk in deceit among your people. You shall not consent to the shedding of your neighbor's blood. I am the Lord your God. You shall not hate your brother in your heart; you shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am the Lord your God. Keep my law." Since you remember that these things are written, do you suppose we would show partiality to your person? You demanded the death of an innocent man, and when you saw yourself disregarded, you exerted yourself to inflict every kind of punishment. God says: "Do not fear the face of the rich man, and you shall honor the face of the elder, and you shall fear the Lord your God. I am the Lord your God." And did you think that you could be feared and that Athanasius, whom God commanded to be honored, could be dishonored? Had you not read that God said: "You shall do no injustice in judgment, in measure, in weight, or in scales; you shall weigh with just scales"? And is it a just measure that you decided an absent man should be put to death by us? If it is a just judgment that a man who cries out to be heard should <not> be heard, and should be punished in his absence, then your accusations against us before God will also be just, since we have spurned the commands of your rashness. In Deuteronomy the glorious Moses is found saying to the judges whom he had given the people: "Hear the cases between your brothers and judge justly between a man and his brother and the stranger who is with him. You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall judge the small as well as the great; you shall not respect any man's person, for the judgment is God's." And you, Constantius—I suppose because you live in royal loftiness—want partiality shown to your person; you are eager for the man whose blood you thirst for to be slaughtered through us, the priests of the Lord. That is why we are detestable to you, because we pronounce judgment according to God's will; that is why you thought you should stretch out your executioner's right hand to the sword, as though you could conquer with the sword those whom you saw neither hesitating to lose this present life for the sake of the Son of God nor dreading death. The most holy Moses tells the children of Israel at God's command: "See, the Lord your God has handed the land over to you before your face; go up and possess it, as the Lord, the God of our fathers, told us. Do not fear or be afraid." If they were commanded to fear no one but God—they who bore the image of our calling—how much more fitting is it that we should fear no one but God, we who desire to gain not the lands of the Canaanites, Jebusites, Girgashites and Amorites, but the heavenly kingdom, God's everlasting love? For how could the force of your empty rank, or how can it now, turn us from this resolve, when we have determined to fear no one but God?

We Christians are not of those who said: "Because the Lord hated us, he brought us out of the land of Egypt, to hand us over to the Amorites and destroy us"; but we are of those who said, and still say, to God: "For your sake we are being killed all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for the slaughter; but in all these things we overcome because of him who loved us." We did not fear, nor do we fear, your threats, we who know that nothing can resist God; we do not want to perish like those who hear from Moses: "Your brothers turned your hearts away, saying, 'The nation is great and very fierce and stronger than you, and the cities are great and walled up to heaven; and we even saw the sons of giants there.'" We Christians do not fear your sword, we who are confident that once you, the enemies of God's religion, have been laid low, we shall come to the banquet of the patriarchs, prophets, apostles and martyrs. We, the soldiers of God, do not fear the might of your perishable kingdom. We are not of those sons of distrust who thought their enemies more powerful than God, that we should dread your frail power. For if the Jews had not believed that the Canaanites, Jebusites, Amorites and their other enemies were more powerful than God, they would surely never have disregarded the voice of Moses saying: "Do not speak so, and do not be afraid of them. The Lord your God, who goes before your face, will himself fight against them together with you, according to all that he did for you in the land of Egypt, and in this desert, where you see how the Lord your God cherished you as a man cherishes his son, all along the way you walked until you came to this place, leading you in fire by night, showing you the road to walk in, and in a cloud by day." If, after these saving warnings, the children of Israel had not believed that those they were fighting were more powerful than God, they would surely never have come to utter destruction. We know, then, that God is powerful to snatch us out of your hands as we make our way toward the heavenly kingdom promised to us. We cannot fear your cruelty, especially since we have chosen to be punished by you rather than by God.

You said: "Condemn Athanasius." Whom were we to condemn, Constantius? Him, whom we see confessing the Son of God, as the patriarchs, prophets, apostles and martyrs confessed him? Or you, who deny him, as your master Arius denied him, as Judas Iscariot and all the Jews denied him? God says to Moses: "You shall have no other gods besides me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or on the earth beneath, or in the waters under the earth. You shall not bow down to them nor serve them, for I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, visiting the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments." And trampling on these divine commands you say: "Accept my idolatry, forsake God, kill Athanasius, who is my enemy, not God's, so that you may be found among those who hate God, whom he has promised to repay to the third and fourth generation; take care not to be loved by God along with those of whom he says, 'showing mercy to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.'" You see, most prudent emperor, that what is evil seems good to you, and what is good seems evil. Will you deny the good, or will you deny that you take good things to be evil and evil things to be good? If you deny it, answer: Is it good or evil to condemn an innocent man? Is it good or evil to forsake God and go after idolatry? If you say it is evil, we will say to you: Then why do you do these things? Again Moses cries out in Deuteronomy, saying: "Keep the commandments of the Lord your God, and the testimonies and ordinances which he has commanded you, and you shall do what is pleasing and good before the Lord your God, so that it may go well with you; and you shall go in and take as your inheritance the good land which the Lord swore to your fathers." And you have chosen as good, as pleasing to God, that idolatry be established by the power of your reign in insult to his majesty, and that those who have confessed themselves his worshipers be slaughtered. "Behold," says Moses, "I have set before you today a blessing and a curse: a blessing, if you hear the commandments of the Lord your God which I command you today." Since, then, those are blessed who do not punish the innocent, and those keep the Lord's commandments who refuse to condemn a man unheard, how can you think yourself blessed, when by your own conduct you prove that you are placed among the cursed? Or, if you are not among the cursed, why do you despise Moses when he says: "If there is found among you, in one of your cities which the Lord your God will give you, a man or a woman who has done evil before the Lord your God by transgressing his covenant, and they have gone and served other gods and worshiped them, or the sun or the moon or anything of the heavens that is in the world," and further on: "you shall bring out that man or that woman, and you shall stone them with stones, and they shall die. On the testimony of two or three witnesses he shall die; he shall not be put to death on the testimony of one witness. And the hand of the witnesses shall be upon him first to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. And you shall remove the evil from among you"? If you are not, Constantius, running with the cursed, why have you not obeyed the commandments of God's servant Moses? Why, when he says that even an idolater is to die only on the testimony of two or three witnesses, did you not even want a hearing granted to a man dedicated to God, and instead had a hearing denied him—the very man into whose charge God has given you, and whom, if you resist him when he defends what is just, you are ordered by the mouth of Moses to be put to death? For so that the judgments of the priest may remain inviolate, he speaks thus: "You shall arise and go up to whatever place the Lord your God chooses for his name to be invoked there. And speak to the priests, the Levites, or to the judge who is in office in those days, and they will inquire and declare the judgment to you; and you shall act according to every instruction that those in the place which the Lord your God has chosen for his name to be invoked there declare to you, and take great care. You shall do according to all that they have laid down for you. According to the law and according to the judgment that they tell you, you shall act; you shall not turn aside from any word that they declare to you; you shall do whatever they show you; you shall not turn aside to the right or to the left. And any man who acts in pride, refusing to listen to the priests who stand to perform their office in the name of the Lord God, or to the judge, whoever he may be in those days, that man shall die, and you shall remove the evil from Israel. And all the people will hear and be afraid, and will no longer act impiously."

But you say: "In this passage Moses, most devoted to God, mentioned the judge just as he mentioned the priests." Then prove that you have been made judge over us. Prove that you were appointed emperor for this purpose: to drive us by your arms to carry out every wish of your friend the devil. Since you cannot prove it, [?]. You have been commanded not only not to lord it over bishops, but also to obey their statutes, so much so that if you tried to overturn their decrees, if you were caught in pride, you were ordered to die the death. How, then, can you say that you are able to judge bishops, when, unless you obey them, you have already, as far as God is concerned, been sentenced to the penalty of death? Since this is so, why do you, a profane man, take upon yourself this authority of God's priests over the household of God? Even the Jews, at the time when they remained in God's law, were allowed by him to have their judges only from their own race. "For if," says Moses, "you say, 'I will set a ruler over me, like the other nations that are around me,' you shall surely set over yourself as ruler whomever the Lord your God chooses. From among your brothers you shall set him. You may not set over yourself a foreigner, since he is not your brother." And he goes on to say why he did not want a foreigner to become ruler: namely, so that he would not draw others into his own sect. That is why he says, "so that he may not lead us back into Egypt," that is, to the worship of idols. Just so you, I say, have usurped for yourself this authority which God did not give you. And even if he had given it and allowed you to be among them, first of all you ought to have been a Christian, because it would be a crime for a foreigner to judge the servants of God, for an enemy of religion to judge the household of God. Then, if you had been a Christian, and God had decided that you should share with the priests in ruling his people, hear what kind of man he commanded you to be: "And when he sits on the throne of his kingdom, he shall write for himself this Deuteronomy in a book before the priests and Levites, and it shall be with him, and you shall read it to him all the days of his life, so that they may learn to fear the Lord your God, to keep all these commandments and to carry out these ordinances, so that his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers, and he may not turn aside from the commandments to the right or to the left, so that he may reign a long time, he and his sons with him, among the children of Israel." What do you have of this kind? Nothing but the opposite in everything, nothing but whatever attacks the house of God! First, you are a heretic; next, a persecutor of God's household. You have tried, and are still trying, to slaughter Athanasius, like a man who does not remember that it is written: "If there is a man who hates his neighbour and lies in wait for him, and rises up against him and strikes him with intent, and he dies, and the man flees into one of these cities, the elders of that city shall send and take him from there and hand him over to those who seek the blood, and he shall die. Your eye shall not spare him, and you shall cleanse the blood of the innocent from among them, and it will be well with you." And again: "A single witness shall not stand to testify against a man for any iniquity or any sin that is committed. At the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand. But if an unjust witness stands up against a man, charging him with iniquity, the two men who have the dispute shall stand before the Lord and before the priest and in the presence of the judge who is in office in those days. And the judges shall inquire diligently, and if the unjust witness has testified wickedly, standing against his brother, then do to him as he wickedly meant to do to his brother, and you shall remove the wicked from among you. And the rest, hearing it, will fear, and will no longer do this evil thing among you. Your eyes shall not spare him: life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot." Since you see that God has decreed these things about you, a murderer, tell me, I pray: what else is it to say, "Condemn the man you know to be innocent, act against God's commandments," than to say, "Tear out your hearts, rid yourselves of your senses, willingly slaughter your own souls; though you see that it is a pit, pretend you are blind and throw yourselves headlong into the eternal abyss; plunge into that pit from which you see you cannot be rescued; take away your own life, take up everlasting death"? What else is it to say, "Do what God has forbidden to be done," than to say, "Be enemies of God, acquire the devil as your friend, take care not to attain paradise, nor in the end the kingdom of heaven which God promised you if you kept his commandments; love hell, cherish the burning lake, long to be with all who are forever paying penalties, long to be called men of the devil"?

These are the rewards that your excellent counsels win; these are those "best" things that give birth to everlasting death; these are what plunge a man already near to heaven down to hell. Did you not yet know what is written, that you should ask us to commit these evils? "There shall not be in your bag two weights, a greater and a smaller. There shall not be in your house two measures, a greater and a smaller. You shall have a true and just weight, and you shall have a true and just measure, so that you may live many days and it may be well with you on the land which the Lord your God will give you as your lot; for everyone who does these things is an abomination to the Lord your God, everyone who does wrong." Since the sacred writings report that whoever has not kept honest weights and just measures is an abomination, I suppose you thought we would be most acceptable if we had pronounced an unjust judgment against him. Moses says, "Cursed is he who moves his neighbour's boundaries." We are forbidden to tear up our neighbour's boundaries and move them from place to place, and [?] the weight; yet you say, "Priests of God, overstep the boundaries of justice." "Cursed," says the Holy Spirit through the mouth of Moses, "is whoever perverts the judgment due to the stranger, the orphan and the widow"; and you, making sport for yourself with our blood, said, "Punish him whom you do not know to have done wrong." We did not want, Constantius, to be accursed with you; rather, we long for you to be found blessed with us in the holy church. We do not listen to your voice, which urges us to incur God's displeasure; we listen to Moses, the servant of the Lord, who says: "And if you do not listen to the voice of the Lord your God, to keep and do all his commandments which I command you today, all these curses shall come upon you and overtake you. Cursed are you in the city, cursed are you in the field; cursed are your storehouses and all that is left to you; cursed are the children of your womb and the produce of your land, the herds of your oxen and the flocks of your sheep; cursed are you in your going. The Lord will send upon you weariness and affliction and anxiety in everything to which you put your hand, whatever you do, until he destroys you swiftly because of the wickedness of your pursuits." If it is not a wicked pursuit to bring false charges, to persecute the worshippers of God, to bring idolatry into God's church, to slaughter by the hand of soldiers those who believe in the only Son of God, then these curses may well fail to overtake you and those who run with you.

You called us together to slaughter a priest of God, to destroy the man through whom God has ordained that you should hear his precepts. "And Moses wrote the words of this law in a book and gave it to the priests and Levites who carry the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and to the elders of Israel. And Moses commanded them on that day, saying: After seven years, at the time of the year of release, at the feast of Tabernacles, when all Israel comes together to appear before the Lord your God in the place which he chooses, you shall read this law before Israel in their hearing, having called together into assembly the men and the women and the children and the proselyte who is in your cities, so that they may hear and learn to fear the Lord your God and listen so as to do all the words of this law. And their children, who do not know, will hear and learn the Lord your God all the days that they live on the land." You persecute the man through whom the Lord commanded you to hear; and while he is still living among men, you send your fellow heretic George as his successor! Yet even if Athanasius had already been freed from the body, you would not have been permitted to send one. It lay, and lies, in the hand of God whom he would deign to appoint as bishop for his people, through his servants, that is, the catholic bishops. For no one could be filled with the power of the Holy Spirit to govern God's people unless he were one whom God had chosen and on whom hands had been laid by catholic bishops. So we find that when Moses died, his successor Joshua the son of Nun was filled with the Holy Spirit, as holy scripture says: "And Joshua the son of Nun was filled with the spirit of understanding, for Moses had laid his hand upon him. And the children of Israel listened to him and did as the Lord had commanded Moses." You see that you have gone against God's ordination by acting against God's will, and that you have slain yourself with the point of your own sword, since no one could lawfully be ordained unless Athanasius had died, and when Athanasius had died, a catholic ought to have been ordained by catholic bishops. Sacred scripture says that God said to Joshua the son of Nun: "Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise, cross the Jordan, you and all this people, into the land which I will give them. Every place on which you set the sole of your foot I will give to you, as I said to Moses. From the desert and Lebanon before it, as far as the great river Euphrates and as far as the great sea, toward the setting of the sun, shall be your borders. No man shall stand against you all the days of your life, and as I was with Moses, so I will be with you, and I will not forsake you nor despise you." Can God be with his enemy George? Can he be gracious to one whom he did not ordain, whom he did not choose? George is just such a man as Arius was, and as Valens and Ursacius are, or Eudoxius of Germanicia, to whom you sent me; for nothing but thorns can come from thorns. That this is so you can gather from the acts of George himself by reading the protests of the Alexandrians. And although it pleases you that he is a wicked blasphemer (for he would not otherwise be so very dear to you, except that he is wicked), still I have brought these things forward so that you may see your outstanding work. Since, then, you recognize that God is not with George, but perceive that he is with Athanasius, whom he appointed bishop for his people, you can at last recognize that you have tried to destroy God's ordination, and that in Athanasius you have persecuted God. For you hear God say to Moses' successor: "As I was with Moses, so I will be with you, and I will not forsake you nor despise you." And see, in another place: "Be strong and act manfully, to keep and do as Moses my servant commanded you. And you shall not turn from it to the right or to the left, so that you may understand in all that you do. And this book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, and you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may take care to do all that is written. Then I will direct your ways, and then you will understand. Behold, I have commanded you: be strong and act manfully; you have no reason to be terrified or afraid, for the Lord your God is with you in every place."

It now remains for you to prove whether what you or George are doing comes from God's commandments. For you hear God promise that he will be with Moses' successor as he was with Moses, provided only that he keeps what is written in the book of the law. If, then, you find nothing written that bids you do these things, your sense of fairness should at last make you see that God is not with you Arians, but that the one who dwells in you is the one who also dwelt in Cain. What cause drove you to do these things, Constantius, that the power of your reign led you into such pride that you resolved to put to death the man whom God chose for himself in the honour of the priesthood? Had you not found it written in the first book of Kingdoms: "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the mighty man glory in his strength, nor the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, to know and understand God and to do judgment and justice in the midst of the earth"? Why did you pass this over, you who ought at all times to do just judgment, and why did you try to force us too to do injustice with you? You had decreed that the catholic should be deposed by us and the heretic established; but when would men of sound mind have done that? For if Eli the priest, because he had set unworthy sons in the honour of the priesthood, heard and suffered what he did from the Lord, what would we deserve to hear and suffer if we condemned a catholic bishop, and him unheard, and allowed George the Arian to become bishop of the Alexandrians? "And there came," it says, "a man of God, and he said: Thus says the Lord: I plainly revealed myself to your father's house, choosing it out of all the tribes of Israel for my priesthood, to go up to my sacrifice and burn incense and carry the ephod. And I gave to your father's house all the grain of the children of Israel for food. Why, then, have you looked upon my incense and my sacrifice with a wicked eye, and honoured your sons more than me, so as to bless them from the beginning in all the sacrifices of Israel before me? Therefore thus says the Lord of Israel: I said that your house and your father's house should walk before me for ever, and now it is not so. Thus says the Lord: Far be it from me; it shall not be so with me, for those who honour me I will honour, and he who despises me shall be brought to nothing. And behold, the days are coming when I will destroy your seed and the seed of your father, and there shall not be an old man in my house all your days; and I will cut off for you a man from my sanctuary, so that his eyes fail and his soul wastes away. And all the multitude of your house that survives shall fall by the sword of men. And this shall be the sign to you, which shall come upon these two sons of yours, Hophni and Phinehas: on one day both shall die by the sword of men." If he received this rebuke from God for his sons, what kind of rebuke would we deserve to receive for you, Constantius? I believe it would have been said to us, "You have honoured Constantius more than me," just as it was said to him that he had honoured his sons more than God. "In what matter?" you ask. Because if we had carried out your orders, we would have been found to have despised the Lord, since George, like the sons of Eli, is a son of pestilence, and you had decided that we should set him in the place of the man of God, Athanasius. Then again, since God says, "He who honours me shall be honoured, and he who despises me shall be brought to nothing," would we have honoured God if we had listened to your sacrilegious voice, raised against his divine commandments? Or would we rather have honoured him if, counting you as nothing, we strove to obey his sacred statutes alone? Meanwhile, rejoice, then, that you are dishonouring God! For you hear him say that all who despise him will come to nothing. Or will you deny that you dishonoured God by removing from their congregations the priests whom he ordained? Or will you deny that you dishonoured the Lord when, against his decrees, you forced his priests to condemn a man absent and unheard? Did you not, then, dishonour God when you did away with the apostolic and evangelical tradition and decreed that all the worshippers of God should hold the idolatry which the devil built up in the heart of Arius?

Since this is so, it will now be for your prudence to weigh what course is to your advantage: whether to correct your errors here, obtain pardon for such great crimes, and resolve to be found among the household of God; or, brought to nothing, as the Lord promises to those who despise him, to begin paying for ever the penalties paid by those whose paths you have chosen to follow. And so that you may see fully what dangers await you because you dishonour the Godhead, hear also what is said to Samuel about the sons of Eli: "And the Lord said to Samuel: Behold, I am carrying out my words in Israel, and both ears of everyone who hears them shall tingle. On that day I will raise up against Eli all that I have spoken concerning his house, and I will accomplish what I foretold to him, for I will take vengeance on his house for ever because of the iniquities of his sons, which I know; for his sons, despising the Lord, spoke evil, and he did not admonish them or chastise them. And now I have sworn to the house of Eli that the iniquity of Eli's house shall never be atoned for by incense or by sacrifices." If these things were promised to Eli because of his sons' offence, what is promised to you for your sacrilege? If these things were promised to him for ever, what is promised to you, who do such great wrongs? If God said that the sons of Eli spoke evil of him, how much more would he say it of you, who have taken up the blasphemy of Arius, plainly in order to attack the faith that the patriarchs, prophets, apostles and all the martyrs held? We beg you, in the midst of all this, to repent of your deeds, considering at least what befell the sons of Eli when they dishonoured God. "Eli," says scripture, "was very old, and his sons had gone their own way, and their way was evil before the Lord. And it came to pass in those days that the foreigners gathered for battle against Israel." And further on: "And the battle turned, and the men of Israel fell before the foreigners, and four thousand men were struck down in the battle line in the field. And the people came into the camp, and the elders of Israel said: Why has the Lord made us fail today before the foreigners? Let us therefore take the ark of the Lord our God from Shiloh, and let it go out in our midst, and it will deliver us from the hands of our enemies. And the people sent to Shiloh, and they brought from there the ark of the Lord, where the cherubim sat. And both sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, went with the ark of God." And further on: "They fought against them, and the men of Israel gave way before the foreigners, and each fled to his tent. And there was a very great slaughter, and thirty thousand men of Israel fell. And the ark of God was captured, and both sons of Eli died." And further on: "And a man came hurrying to Eli and said: I am the one who has come from the camp; I fled from the battle today. And Eli said: What has happened, my son? And the man answered and said: The men of Israel have fled before the foreigners, and there has been a great slaughter among the people, and both your sons are dead, and the ark of God has been captured. And when he heard that the ark of God had been captured, he fell backward from his seat beside the gate, and his back was broken, and he died, for he was an old man and heavy; and he had judged Israel for twenty years." If these evils came in a single day upon Eli, priest and judge of the Israelites, because he had not chastised his sons as was fitting, I have thought it right to show you at this point what you can see will come upon you, the destroyer of God's religion. For you will not deny that you said it comes from God's will that we, his servants, are subjected to you, our persecutors: "Unless our faith, that is, the one which Lucifer calls Arian, were catholic, I would never have received power over all the peoples." If that is so, then the faith of those foreigners who captured the ark of God must also have been better than that of God's worshippers.

You say that your faith, which we know to be heretical, gave you this. But Maxentius, Nero and all those persecutors of God's house also said that it was by the power of their gods that we Christians came under their rule. Run through what happened to those who rejoiced that they had captured the ark of God, who said that they had defeated the Israelites by the might of their gods, and you will find that you are one of those who persecuted the house of God. "And the foreigners took the ark of God from Ebenezer and brought it into Azotus. And the foreigners took up the ark and brought it into the house of Dagon, and set it beside Dagon. And in the morning the people of Azotus rose early, and went into the house of Dagon and looked. And behold, Dagon had fallen on his face before the ark of God. And they took Dagon up and set him in his place. And the hand of the Lord was heavy upon the people of Azotus, and tormented them. And he struck them in their houses, in Azotus and its territories [?]. And it came to pass, when they rose before dawn, that Dagon had fallen on his face before the ark of the Lord's covenant, and the head of Dagon and both the palms of his hands had been cut off in a hundred pieces, and both the joints [?] of his hands had fallen on the threshold." And further on: "And the hand of the Lord was heavy upon Azotus, and he brought mice upon them, and there was a great confusion of death in the city. And the men of Azotus saw that it was so, and they said, 'The ark of the Lord God of Israel shall not stay with us, for his hand is hard upon us and upon Dagon our god.' And they sent and called the lords of the foreigners to them and said, 'What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?' And the men of Gath said, 'Let the ark of the God of Israel pass over to Gath.' And it came to pass, after the ark of God had been carried over, that the hand of the Lord was upon the city, and there was a very great disturbance. And he struck the men of the city from the least to the greatest, and mice broke out upon them in their seats, and the men of Gath made themselves seats of skin, and they sent the ark of God to Ascalon. And it came to pass, when the ark of the God of Israel entered Ascalon, that the people of Ascalon cried out, saying, 'Why have you sent the ark of the God of Israel to us, to hand us and our people over to death?' And they sent and called the lords of the foreigners and said, 'Send back the ark of the God of Israel, and let it be taken back to its place, and it will not hand us and our people over to death'; for a heavy confusion had come upon the whole city, very heavy, when the ark of God entered it. And those who lived and did not die were struck in their seats, and the cry of the cities went up to heaven." You see, Constantius, how our God allows his religion to appear humbled by you foreigners, and humbled to this extent, until even you persecutors of the true religion see that there is no other God besides our God.

But to return once more to the case of Athanasius: did you not know that it is written in the first book of Kingdoms, "And Samuel judged the people of Israel in all holiness," that you should think it right to command that an innocent man be condemned by the Lord's priests? You have read that Samuel judged God's people in all holiness; and because we refuse to depart from this just way of judging, we suffer persecution from you. This is nothing new, since Saul persecuted the righteous Samuel because he told him the truth—and that was the very man through whom he had been anointed king, through whom the Lord had raised him to such great glory. Saul persecuted the Lord's prophet and priest because he was not in his right mind; otherwise, how could Saul, if he were sound, persecute a man whom he knew to be God's minister, full of God's Spirit? He persecuted the man who, though Saul did not know it, had groaned continually for the welfare of his persecutor. Scripture tells in the first book of Kingdoms that the Lord said to Samuel: "How long will you mourn for Saul? Behold, I am casting him out, so that he may not reign over Israel. Fill your horn with oil and come; I will send you to the house of Jesse in Bethlehem, for I have seen among the sons of Jesse a king for myself." And Samuel said, "How can I go? Saul will hear of it and kill me." Saul was seeking to destroy the man whom he remembered, in many ways, to be a man of God. The man of God does not cease asking pardon for his persecutor; on the contrary, the one who has become a son of pestilence seeks to take away his life. Indeed, Saul became so great a persecutor of Samuel, the Lord's priest, that when the Lord said to him, "Come, I will send you," Samuel replied, "And how can I go? Saul will hear and kill me." You see, Constantius, that when you withdraw from God you are reckoned not as men but as wild animals, as beasts and robbers. Or will you not be compared with Saul in this, that you unjustly persecute Athanasius? For you are as eager to butcher the innocent Athanasius as he was eager to kill not only Samuel but David too. Saul threatened to kill precisely those with whom he knew God to be. "And Saul saw," says Scripture, "that the Lord was with David, and all Israel loved him. And Saul grew still more afraid of David. And Saul spoke to Jonathan his son and to all his servants about killing David." Answer, most shameless emperor: can someone who has the Spirit of God do such things? At what time did Saul begin to do them? Surely when he was cursed and rejected through Samuel; for at that very time it is written that God departed from him and was with David. By these things it is proved that you Arians are without the Spirit of God, you who persecute Athanasius, a man full of the Holy Spirit. "And David," it says, "was wise in all his ways, and the Lord was with him, and all Israel and Judah loved David." So that you may recognize that you are doing to Athanasius what Saul did to David, take what is written: "And Jonathan the son of Saul loved David greatly, and Jonathan told David, saying, 'Saul is seeking to kill you.'" And further on: "And Jonathan spoke to his father, saying, 'Do not sin, O king, against your servant David, for he has not sinned against you, and his deeds are very good. He put his life in his hands and killed the foreigner, and the Lord wrought salvation in Israel, and all Israel saw it and rejoiced. Why then do you sin against innocent blood, and kill David without cause?' And Saul heard the voice of Jonathan his son, and Saul swore, saying, 'As the Lord lives, David shall not be put to death.'" And further on: "And war broke out again, and David prevailed and fought the foreigners and struck them with a great blow, and they fled before David. And an evil spirit came upon Saul, and he was sleeping in his house, and there was a spear in his hand, and behold, David was playing music with his hands. And Saul sought to strike David with the spear, and he struck, and David moved away from Saul. And he struck the spear into the wall, and David fled and was saved. And that night Saul sent messengers to David's house to guard him, so that he might kill him in the morning. And David fled and was saved. And he came to Samuel at Ramathaim and told him all that Saul had done." And further on: "And Saul was very angry with Jonathan." And further on: "And he said, 'Leave this; fetch the young man, for he is a son of death.' And Jonathan answered his father, 'Why should he die? What has he done?' And Saul raised his spear against Jonathan to kill him." Whom would Saul spare among those who told him the truth, when he did not spare even his son? So you too pass over the commandments of God and establish your own. In short, we are not surprised if you persecute the Lord's priests because it is said that an absent man cannot be condemned, since we see that Saul likewise persecuted those who served God. Scripture speaks, saying: "And the king said, 'You shall surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father's house.'" And further on: "And the king said to the runners and to those standing by him, 'Bring the priests of the Lord and kill them, for their hand is with David; for they knew that David was fleeing and did not disclose it to me.' And the king's servants would not lay their hands on the priests of the Lord."

What do you say, most just king? If the king's servants are recorded as refusing to obey the king's command, if they are shown to have despised Saul's orders so as not to act against God's commandments, was it right for us bishops to trample on the Lord's precepts and carry out yours—the orders of a sacrilegious murderer? This, then, is why you see fit to persecute us: because we do not put your commands before the Lord's. Saul did these things too, as sacred Scripture proves, saying: "And Saul said to Doeg, 'Turn and fall upon the priests of the Lord.' And Doeg the Syrian turned and himself put the priests of the Lord to death, and on that day he killed three hundred and five men, all who wore the ephod; and at Nob, the city of the priests, he killed with the edge of the sword, from man to nursing infant." In the same way you have tried, and are trying now, to tear apart the bodies of those whom you see resisting your command because they remember God's commands. So we cannot be surprised if you persecute us, since we see that Saul, because they had not delivered the Lord's servant David into his hands, destroyed not only three hundred and five priests but a whole city. Saul persecuted David, the man who often spared him even when Saul was in his power. "And it came to pass," says Scripture, "when Saul had returned from pursuing the foreigners, that they told him, saying, 'Behold, David is in the wilderness of Azotus.' And he took with him three thousand chosen men out of all Israel, and went to seek David and his men in front of the stags' hunting ground. And he came to the sheepfolds that were by the road, and there was a cave there, and Saul went in to relieve himself; and David and his men were sitting in the inner part of the cave. And David's men said to him, 'Behold, this is the day of which the Lord said, "I will give your enemy into your hands, and you shall do to him what seems good in your eyes."' And David rose and secretly cut off the edge of Saul's cloak. And afterward David's heart struck him because he had cut off the edge of the cloak. And David said to his men, 'The Lord forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the Lord's anointed, to lay my hand on him, for he is the Lord's anointed.' And David persuaded his men with words and did not allow them to rise up and kill Saul. And Saul rose and went down to the road, and David went out after Saul, saying, 'My lord the king!' And Saul looked behind him, and David bowed with his face to the ground and did homage to him. And David said to Saul, 'Why do you listen to the words of people who say, "Behold, David seeks your life"? Behold, this day your eyes have seen how the Lord delivered you today into my hands in the cave, and I would not kill you; I spared you and said, "I will not lay my hand on my lord, for he is the Lord's anointed." I took the edge of your cloak in my hand; I cut off the fringe of your cloak and did not kill you. Know and see today that there is no malice or injustice in my hand, and I have not sinned against you, yet you seek to take my life. May the Lord judge between me and you, and he will avenge me on you, but my hand shall not be upon you. As the ancient proverb says, "From the wicked comes wickedness." But my hand shall not be upon you. After whom are you pursuing? After a dead dog? After a single flea? May the Lord be judge and avenger between me and you; may the Lord see and judge my cause and vindicate me from your hand.'" Such is the way of God's worshippers: to leave everything to God, knowing that it is a great thing to be avenged by him.

Meanwhile, as I said above, see what Saul says when he is in his right mind, and how, when he loses it, he thirsts for the blood of David, a righteous and innocent man. "And it came to pass," it says, "when David had finished speaking these words to Saul, that Saul said, 'Is this your voice, my son David?' And Saul cried aloud and wept. And he said to David, 'You are more righteous than I, for you have repaid me with good, but I have repaid you with evil. And today you have told me the good you have done me, how the Lord shut me up in your hands and you did not kill me. As when a man finds his friend and sends him on his way in peace, so may the Lord repay you with good for what you have done to me today. And now, behold, I know that you shall surely reign, and the kingdom of Israel shall be established in your hand. So now swear to me by the Lord that you will not root out my offspring after me and will not destroy my name from my father's house.' And David swore to Saul." After this Saul surely ought to have changed; yet still he does not stop persecuting, nor does David stop sparing him. "And Saul rose," says Scripture, "and went down into the shady wilderness, and with him three thousand chosen men of Israel, to seek David." And further on: "And David sent out scouts and learned that Saul had come to Ziklag. And David rose secretly and went to the place where Saul was sleeping, and Abner the son of Ner, the commander of his army. And Saul was sleeping on splendid coverlets, and the people were around him. And David spoke to Amalech the Gittite and to Abishai the son of Zeruiah, the brother of Joab, saying, 'Who will go into the camp with me to Saul?' And Abishai said to David, 'I will go with you.' And David and Abishai came to the people by night, and behold, Saul was sleeping on costly coverlets, with his splendid spear stuck in the ground at his head, and Abner was sleeping around him. And Abishai said to David, 'Today the Lord has shut up your enemy in your hands. Now let me pin him to the ground with the spear at one stroke, and I will not strike him twice.' And David said to Abishai, 'Do not touch him; for who can lay his hand on the Lord's anointed and be guiltless?' And David said, 'As the Lord lives, unless the Lord strikes him, or his hour comes and he dies, or he goes down into battle and is gathered to his fathers—the Lord forbid that I should lay my hand on the Lord's anointed. Now take the spear that is at his head and the flask of water, and let us go.' And David took the spear and the flask of water from his head, and they went away. And there was no one who saw, no one who knew, and no one awake; for they were all asleep, because a dread from the Lord had fallen upon them. And David crossed over to the other side and stood on the top of a mountain far off, and there was a great distance between them. And David called out to the people and to Abner, and spoke, saying, 'Will you not answer, Abner?' And Abner answered and said, 'Who are you that call me? What is it?' And David said to Abner, 'Are you not a man? And who is like you in Israel? Why have you not guarded your lord the king? For one of the people came in to destroy your lord the king. This thing you have done is not good. As the Lord lives, you are sons of death, because you have not guarded your lord the king, the Lord's anointed. And now look: where is the king's spear, and the flask of water that was at his head?' And King Saul recognized David's voice and said, 'Is this your voice, my son David?' 'It is your servant, my lord the king.' And David added, 'Why is my lord pursuing his servant like this? What wrong have I done, and what malice is in me? Now let my lord the king hear the words of his servant: if it is the Lord God who stirs you up to my grief, then let there be a sacrificial victim [?]; but if it is the sons of men, cursed are they before the Lord, for they have driven me out today so that I am not established in the Lord's inheritance, saying, "Go, serve other gods." Now let not my blood fall to the earth before the Lord, for the king of Israel has come out to seek a single flea, as the owl hunts in the mountains.' And Saul said, 'I have sinned. Come back, my son David, for I will do you no more harm, since my life was precious in your eyes this day; I have acted foolishly and have been exceedingly ignorant in many things.' And David answered, saying, 'Here is the king's spear; let one of the young men come over and take it. And may the Lord repay each man for his righteousness and his faithfulness; for the Lord delivered you into my hands today, and I would not lay my hand on the Lord's anointed. Behold, as your life was exalted this day in my eyes, so may my life be marked out [?] in the sight of the Lord, and may he snatch me away and deliver me from all tribulations.' And Saul said to David, 'Blessed are you, my son; you will surely do great things and will surely prevail.'"

I have set these things down so that at last you might perceive that you are persecuting Athanasius and us just as unjustly, that you are being goaded to the destruction of your own salvation, and that you are bringing upon yourself the peril of death before God, just as Saul brought it on himself by what he did. If this is not so, tell us why you persecute us. Surely it is because we do not shed innocent blood. Whom do you want us to imitate, you or David? For about David I find it written: "And David reigned over Israel, and he executed judgment and justice among all his people." But we see that you are an unjust judge, a killer of God's worshippers. Why do you persecute us? Surely because we refused to become apostates, as you are, because we refused to deny the only Son of God. The book of David speaks of the perfect Trinity and proclaims one Godhead of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit; and you are found to be an apostate. Whom, I ask, shall I follow, you or David? That worshipper of the Lord, that lover of mercy, or you, a sacrilegious butcher? What sort of wisdom does a man have who persecutes Athanasius? I would be amazed at your doing these things if King Ahab had not likewise persecuted Elijah and the other prophets of the Lord; I would be amazed at your persecuting a man of God if I did not see that you are Ahab in every respect. In short, we say to you the same kind of things that were said to him by the members of God's household: "Do not worship Baal, do not serve idols, but serve God; serve the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob; serve the God of Israel." If you remember that Elijah and the other prophets of the Lord said such things to Ahab, the apostate king, take note that similar things are being said to you by those to whom the Lord has given authority to teach. Do not, Constantius, fight alongside the Arians against the house of God; do not bring the idolatry of Arius into the Church; do not deny the only Son of God; stop persecuting the apostolic and evangelical faith. Because we say these things, we seem to you to be your enemies. So too those who told the king the truth were his enemies. Let us run through, then, what arose and what took place between Elijah, the Lord's prophet, and Ahab, your fellow apostate, and you will find that today you are Ahab. "As the Lord lives," says Elijah, "before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain in these years except by the word of my mouth." When this had indeed been fulfilled, the madman ought to have recognized that truly no one but the God whom Elijah served was the only and all-powerful God. What does Ahab do? He sees that there has been no rain for three years and more, and he grows all the more devoted to idols, all the more eager to kill Elijah. The prophet of God hears from the mouth of the sacrilegious Ahab: "Is it you, you who overturn Israel?" So you too say to Athanasius and to us that it is we who are overturning God's people, when it is you who are summoning Christians to take up your heresy. But you hear from us what that idolatrous Ahab heard from the glorious Elijah: "It is not we who are overturning the house of God, but you and your father's house." Or will you deny that you think of nothing but making us all your fellow apostates?

But to return to what I had begun to say about the deeds of Elijah and Ahab: And Elijah said, “It is not I who overturn Israel, but you and your father's house, because you forsake the Lord our God and go after Baal. Now send and gather all Israel to me at Mount [?], with the four hundred and fifty prophets of shame and the four hundred prophets of the groves, who eat and drink at Jezebel's table.” And King Ahab sent to all Israel and gathered all the prophets to Mount Carmel. And Elijah [?] came near to them all and said to them, “How long will you limp in your minds? If the Lord is God, go after him; but if Baal is, go after him.” And the people did not answer him a word. And Elijah [?] spoke to the people, saying, “I alone am left, the only one of the Lord's prophets, and the prophets of this Baal are four hundred and fifty men, and the prophets of the groves four hundred. So let two bulls be given to us; let them choose one for themselves, cut it in pieces and lay it on the wood, but put no fire under it; and I will prepare the other bull and put no fire under it. Then call on the name of your gods, and I will call on the name of my God; and whichever answers us by fire, he shall be God.” And all the people answered and said, “What Elijah has said is good.” And Elijah said to the prophets of shame, “Choose one calf for yourselves and go first, since you are many, and call on the name of your gods, but put no fire under it.” And they took the calf and prepared it, and called on the name of Baal from morning until evening, saying, “Hear us, Baal, hear us.” But there was no voice and no hearing. And Elijah the Tishbite added, saying, “Call out together with a loud voice; perhaps he is busy, or asleep, and he will be woken.” And they called on him with a loud voice, and cut themselves with swords and razors, as was their custom, until the blood poured out over them, and they went on prophesying until midday had passed. And when the time came for offering the sacrifice, Elijah the Tishbite spoke to the prophets, saying, “Stand aside now, and I will prepare the burnt offering.” And they stood aside and went away. And Elijah said to the people, “Come near to me.” And all the people came near to him, and Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of Israel, as the Lord had spoken to him, saying, “Israel shall be your name.” And he built the stones and repaired the altar of the Lord that had been torn down, and made a trench around the altar that would hold two measures of seed, and he piled split wood on the altar he had made, and cut up the burnt offering and laid it on the wood and piled it on the altar. And he said, “Bring me four jars of water and pour them over the burnt offering and over the wood.” And he said, “Bring more again.” And they brought more again. And he said, “Do it a third time.” And they did it a third time, and the water ran all round the altar, and they filled the trench with water. And Elijah cried out to heaven and said, “Lord God of Abraham and Isaac and Israel, hear me, Lord, hear me today by fire, so that all this people may know that you are the Lord God of [?], and I am your servant, and that I have done these works for your sake; and it is you who have turned the heart of this people back.” And fire fell from the Lord out of heaven and consumed the burnt offerings and the wood and the water that was in the [?], and the stones and the earth; the fire licked them up. And all the people fell on their faces and said, “Truly the Lord God, he is God.” And Elijah said to the people, “Seize the prophets of Baal; let not one of them escape.” And they seized them, and Elijah brought them down to the brook Kishon and killed them there. And he said to Ahab, “Eat and drink, for there is the sound of the feet of rain.” And Ahab went up to eat and drink. And Elijah went up to Carmel, and bowed down to the ground and put his face between his knees, and said to his servant, “Go up and look toward the sea.” And the servant looked, and the servant said, “There is nothing.” “Go back seven times.” And at the seventh time, behold, a small cloud like a man's footprint, bringing water from the sea. And Elijah said to him, “Go up and say to Ahab, ‘Harness your chariot and go up, so that the rain does not overtake you.’” And meanwhile the sky grew black with clouds and wind, and there was a great rain. And Ahab went weeping into Israel, and the hand of the Lord was on Elijah.

You see in what perversity you remain today, the very perversity in which Ahab remained. For after such great signs and wonders had been shown, he would not deign to rejoice with the people, but grieved that Elijah had dared to kill the priests and prophets of the idols; nor after all this would he deign to turn to God, but instead he persecuted God's worshipper all the more. He sees that God is in Elijah, and he seeks his life all the more. He perceives that the prophets of Baal and of the groves were worshippers of demons, and he loves them, even dead, more than the one he had found in so many ways to be of God's household. In just the same way you deign to love those whom you see to be men of the Arian heresy, and you persecute the worshippers of God as fiercely as you can. I have chosen to set before you a few of the many things that passed between Ahab and Elijah so that you may recognize that you [?], ever since you abandoned God, are not easily converted to him by signs or wonders, but rather persist in your errors and rage like savage beasts against the necks of God's worshippers. We beg you, Constantius, do not choose to linger any longer in these evils of yours, but rather break free from the whirlwinds of the devil, so that the evils that overtook Ahab and Jezebel may not overtake you. And do not call yourself fortunate because you have the power to persecute God's people, when you see that Ahab and Jezebel could have been destroyed at Elijah's request, and yet were spared, so that the patience of Elijah, the man of God, might be more fully blessed, and the measure of their wickedness filled up. As if Elijah could not have asked God that the persecutors of his religion, the worshippers of idols, should burn! He asks for fire to be given from heaven to consume the sacrifices, and at once it comes down; he asks for the rain that had been withheld for three years and six months, and at once it is given; very many other signs are performed. Could God's enemies not have been destroyed at Elijah's request, when fire came down at Elijah's word and consumed even those honoured captains of fifty? You can see that today too you could be destroyed by a thunderbolt, or in any way at all, for persecuting Athanasius and us; but you are being spared so that either you may turn, or the whole measure of your wickedness may be filled up. King Ahab persecuted Elijah, as you now persecute Athanasius. Indeed, after Jezebel learned that those mighty works had been shown through Elijah and that the prophets of shame and the priests of the cults had been killed, she said to the Lord's prophet: “May the gods do this to me and more besides, if by this hour tomorrow I have not made your life like the life of one of them.” But what does Elijah hear from God after keeping a fast of forty days and nights? That he should anoint kings by whom Ahab and his allies would be destroyed. God's mercy is with Elijah; Elijah knows that he is loved by God. Ahab, on the other hand, Elijah's persecutor, is so wretched that he was always in the devil's power. You have ordered Athanasius to be “justly” punished in just the way that Jezebel ordered Naboth the Jezreelite to be; you have produced “true” witnesses against Athanasius just as those did to whom Jezebel had written, saying: “Proclaim a fast, and seat Naboth at the head of the people, and set two men, sons of the wicked, against him, and let them testify against him, saying, ‘You have cursed the Lord and the king’; and take him out, and let him be stoned and die.”

Such now are your works, you Arians. You call us guilty, you heap many charges on us, and you have no need of false witnesses, for you yourselves are false witnesses in everything. In this way you Arians, sons of perdition, are trying to kill Athanasius, just as Jezebel killed Naboth, as though you could escape the hand of him who sees all things. You know that God avenged the blood of Naboth and required his death at the hands of those who killed him; and do you suppose that God will not require the blood of his priest Athanasius at your hands? And the Lord said to Elijah the Tishbite: “Arise and go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who is in Samaria, for he has gone down to Naboth's vineyard to take possession of it. And you shall say to him, ‘Thus says the Lord: Because you have killed Naboth and taken possession of his vineyard, therefore thus says the Lord: In the place where dogs and pigs licked up the blood of Naboth, there dogs shall lick up your blood, and harlots shall wash in your blood.’” And Ahab said to Elijah, “Have you found me, my enemy?” And Elijah said, “I have found you, because you have set yourself to do evil in the sight of the Lord, to provoke him. Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will bring evils upon you, and I will kindle a fire after you, and I will destroy from Ahab [?] everyone who pisses against the wall, both the one shut up and the one left in Israel. And I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat, and like the house of Baasha son of Ahijah, for all the provocations with which you have provoked me and made Israel sin.” And to Jezebel the Lord spoke, saying, “Dogs shall eat her by the wall of Jezreel, and the birds shall eat your dead in the city [?].” What do you say to this, Constantius? Do you claim that your sins are less than those of Ahab and Jezebel? They persecuted God's priests, killed those of God's household, did away with the religion of God and set up idolatry, and turned the people away from God. And you have done and are doing all these things. You call us your enemies just as Ahab called Elijah his enemy, who, when he heard the Lord's indignation from the prophet's mouth, said: “Have you found me [?], enemy of King Ahab?” —because, of course, Elijah said, “Do not serve idols, but the one God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel.” And now [?], because you are told, “Do not be a heretic, but be a Christian,” you call us enemies for pressing upon you, as you hand down idolatry, the very things Elijah pressed upon King Ahab. Ahab would surely have loved Elijah if the Lord's prophet had decided that his idols should be served and God abandoned. And you cannot deny just as much: that if we had chosen to be what you yourself are [?], you would have loved us with singular affection. By these things you are shown to be a son of pestilence, a fountain of darkness, the kindling of all evils, the head and whirlpool [?] of wickedness, the cesspool of all blasphemers, the kindling of heretics, a root of bitterness, a tree destined for the fire, since it bears deadly fruit; an enemy of God, a foe of the Church, a falsifier of truth, an inciter [?] of depravity, a lover of injustice, an adversary of [?] justice; turned into darkness, and inextricable darkness at that; made, in truest truth, a temple of all the demons, at whose prompting you, like Ahab, have perpetrated and are perpetrating all these evils. But unless you turn to God, you will not be able to go unpunished for long, when you see what Ahab and Jezebel received. For if Ahab perishes, as had been promised him by Elijah's mouth, if dogs eat Jezebel, will you go unpunished for such great crimes? You who not only feel no grief at having killed those devoted to God, but even glory in it, thinking you have done well. Nor is this surprising, since he who foreknows the future, whom you deny [?], said in the Gospel: “The hour will come when everyone who kills you will think he is offering service to God; but they do this because they know neither the Father nor his only Son.”

Knowingly, living without knowledge of God, you persecute Athanasius, who tells you the truth and loves God with his whole heart. So Ahab too persecuted Elijah. But see the end of Elijah and of his enemy Ahab. Look at Elijah, taken up to enjoy God's friendship for ever, while Ahab is now tormented in the outer darkness. Elijah rejoices in God's friendship, and Ahab pays an everlasting penalty. Athanasius will without doubt be at the banquet where Elijah is; and you, unless you look to your own good, will be in that place of torments where Ahab is held, whom you are found to imitate in everything. Is this wisdom, to choose the eternal misery of King Ahab rather than to enjoy the everlasting happiness that Elijah attained? Scripture speaks of his being taken up in the fourth book of Kingdoms, saying: “And as they went on and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire, and it separated the two of them. And Elijah went up in a whirlwind as if into heaven. And Elisha saw it, and he cried out and said, ‘Father, father, charioteer of Israel!’ And he saw him no more.” What you, a heretic, have done cannot seem new to us when you persecute us, the Lord's priests, since we find in the second book of Chronicles that Jeroboam and his sons did the same. Holy Scripture says: “Judah and Benjamin, and the Levites and the priests who were in all Israel, came together from all their territories, because the Levites left their dwellings and their possessions and went to Rehoboam, since Jeroboam and his sons drove them out so that they should not serve the Lord. And he appointed there priests for the high places and for the idols and the demons and the calves that Jeroboam had made. And he cast out from the sons of Israel and from the tribes of Israel those who had set their hearts to seek the Lord God of Israel.” So it will be no wonder if you persecute us and those entrusted to us by God, if you drive us from the charge entrusted to us, if, in short, you install in our places God's enemies, who have abandoned God along with you, when you see that you are carrying out what Jeroboam did. For what is it to say, “Condemn the faith written down at Nicaea and accept mine,” but what Jeroboam said: “Abandon God and serve my idols”? What sort of man says, “Condemn an innocent man, absent and unheard”? Surely the one who had already denied the apostolic and evangelical faith; the one, in fact, who had destroyed, as far as it lay with you and yours, the tradition of the blessed apostles. That, in the end, is how you came to such madness: because, like Jeroboam, you were without God. For if you had had God, if you had remembered that you were his worshipper, you would certainly never say, “Condemn an innocent man, strike down your fellow priest, absent and unheard.”

And so that you may see that you are without God, which is why you order such things to be done, consider a king with whom his God was present as his merits deserved; consider too his appeal to the Lord's priests, whom he urged to judge just judgment for God's people; look also at the conduct of the judges you have set up against the Church and of their ministers; and you will be able to weigh whether the unclean spirits that were with Jeroboam are not with you. “And Jehoshaphat,” it says in the second book of Chronicles, “dwelt in Jerusalem [?], and he turned and went out among the people from Beersheba to Mount Ephraim, and turned them back to the Lord God of their fathers. And he appointed judges in all the fortified cities of Judah, city by city. He said to the judges, ‘Take heed what you do, for you will judge not for man but for the Lord, and he is with you in the giving of judgment. Now let the fear of the Lord be upon you, and keep it and act on it; for with the Lord our God there is no iniquity, no respect of persons, no taking of bribes.’ And in Jerusalem too Jehoshaphat appointed some of the Levites and priests and heads of Israel for the judgment of the Lord and to judge those who lived in Jerusalem. And he charged them, saying, ‘You shall act thus in the fear of the Lord, with a perfect heart; and in every case that comes before you from your brothers who live in their cities, between blood and blood, between law, commandments, ordinances and judgments, you shall make it clear to them, so that they do not sin against the Lord, and wrath does (not) come upon you and your brothers. Do this and you will not sin. See, Amariah the chief priest is over you in every matter of the Lord, and Zebadiah son of Ishmael, who is ruler of the house of Judah, in every matter of the king, and the scribes and Levites are before you. Be strong and act, and the Lord will be with you for good.’” Did he say to the Lord's priests, or to the princes of his kingdom, or to the other judges, “Condemn the just, persecute the innocent, condemn and kill all who believe in God”? Did he say, “Love what God does not love, hate justice, love injustice,” as you do? Or can you deny that you said, “Condemn Athanasius, absent and unheard”? Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, devoted to God, says that judgment must be according to the Lord's law; and you, a king turned to apostasy, say, “Condemn a man unheard.”

Suppose for a moment, Constantius, that King Jehoshaphat were alive in the body today, and that each of you were speaking to us: he saying, “Take heed what you do, for you will judge not for man but for the Lord, and he is with you in the giving of judgment. Now let the fear of the Lord be upon you, so that you keep it and act on it; for with the Lord our God there is no iniquity, no respect of persons”; and you, on the contrary, saying that a man must be condemned unheard, and a man whom you yourself know to be innocent at that. Which of you could we have obeyed, we bishops of God, we whom he had long ago promised to his people through the mouth of Jeremiah, saying: “And I will give you shepherds after my own heart, and they will feed you, shepherding you with discipline”? Which, I say, should we obey: you, or Jehoshaphat, a man devoted to God, who would compel us to do what we remembered God had commanded to be done? If, then, you recognize that he made it his rule to fulfil the Lord's commandments, while you have turned out to be not only a destroyer of God's commandments but even a deserter of God himself, it remains for you to see which of you was a man of God, which of you did the will of his mercy. We read it written of him thus: “And the Lord was with Jehoshaphat, because he walked in the earlier ways of his father, and did not seek idols, but the Lord God of his father, and walked in his commandments, and not according to the works of Israel. And the Lord established his kingdom, and all Judah brought Jehoshaphat gifts, and he had great riches and glory. And his heart was lifted up in the ways of the Lord, and furthermore he cut down the groves from Judah.
